1.q: וַ⁠יֹּ֧סֶף אַבְרָהָ֛ם וַ⁠יִּקַּ֥ח אִשָּׁ֖ה וּ⁠שְׁמָ֥⁠הּ קְטוּרָֽה
1.note: Abraham probably married Keturah after Sarah died (Genesis [23:1–2](ta:23)) and after Isaac married Rebekah (Genesis 24:67). Make sure your translation of this verse does not sound like Abraham had two wives named Keturah. Alternate translation: [Then Abraham married another woman, who was named Keturah]

2.note: See how you translated **bore for him** in Genesis 21:3; 24:47. Alternate translation: [Keturah gave birth to sons for him whose names were] or [She bore sons for him whom they named] or [They had sons together whom they named]

2.q: אֶת־זִמְרָן֙ וְ⁠אֶת־יָקְשָׁ֔ן וְ⁠אֶת־מְדָ֖ן וְ⁠אֶת־מִדְיָ֑ן וְ⁠אֶת־יִשְׁבָּ֖ק וְ⁠אֶת־שֽׁוּחַ
2.note: See how you used commas and conjunctions in similar lists of names in Genesis 22:22, 24.

3.note: See how you translated **fathered** in Genesis 11:27. Alternate translation: [Jokshan was the father of]
Alternate translation: [sons whom they named Sheba and Dedan]

3.q: וּ⁠בְנֵ֣י דְדָ֔ן הָי֛וּ אַשּׁוּרִ֥ם וּ⁠לְטוּשִׁ֖ים וּ⁠לְאֻמִּֽים
3.note: See how you translated the names of people groups in Genesis 10:4, 13–14, 16–18, and see the note about that at 10:4.

4.note: Consider what is the best way to connect the names in this list in your language.

This phrase refers back to all the people listed in verses 2–4, which includes Keturah’s six sons, seven grandsons and three great grandsons. Make sure you spelled **Keturah** consistently in [verses 1–4](ta:25). Alternate translation: [All those were the descendants of Keturah and Abraham]

5.note: Some languages have a specific word such as “left” or “willed” that means to give something as an inheritance. In that time and culture, a father would give his children their inheritance before he died. Alternate translation: [Abraham willed everything that he owned to Isaac] or [And Isaac inherited all that Abraham owned]

6.q: וְ⁠לִ⁠בְנֵ֤י הַ⁠פִּֽילַגְשִׁים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לְ⁠אַבְרָהָ֔ם נָתַ֥ן אַבְרָהָ֖ם מַתָּנֹ֑ת
6.note: See how you translated **concubine** in Genesis 22:24. The word **gifts** in this clause is very general and can include domestic animals, servants, gold, silver, and other things. Alternate translation: [Abraham also gave valuable gifts to the sons he had with his concubines] or [Abraham also gave (valuable gifts) to the sons that his servant wives had for him]

6.q: וַֽ⁠יְשַׁלְּחֵ֞⁠ם & בְּ⁠עוֹדֶ֣⁠נּוּ חַ֔י קֵ֖דְמָ⁠ה אֶל־אֶ֥רֶץ קֶֽדֶם
6.note: The Hebrew word **Kedem** means “east” and refers to the region east of Canaan and the Dead Sea. Consider whether it is best in your language to transliterate (copy) the Hebrew name or to translate the meaning. Alternate translation: [then while he was still alive he sent them eastward to the region in the East] or [but after that he sent them to the east country] or [and after that he made them move away to the east country]
Alternate translation: [to be far away from his son Isaac] or [so that they would be far away from his son Isaac]

7.q: וְ⁠אֵ֗לֶּה יְמֵ֛י שְׁנֵֽי־חַיֵּ֥י אַבְרָהָ֖ם אֲשֶׁר־חָ֑י מְאַ֥ת שָׁנָ֛ה וְ⁠שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וְ⁠חָמֵ֥שׁ שָׁנִֽים
7.note: Alternate translation: [Abraham lived a total of 175 years]

8.note: Alternate translation: [Then he breathed out for the last time] or [Then he took his final breath]
Alternate translation: [and died at a ripe old age] or [and died when he was very old]

The idiom **full** refers to a long life that was blessed by God. Consider what is the best way to translate this idiom in your language. Alternate translation: [an old man who had lived a full life, and] or [After he had lived a long and blessed life]

The phrase **gathered to his people** is a euphemism that refers to dying but also implies that God took his spirit to be with his ancestors who had already died. It is best to translate this phrase fairly literally since it teaches about life after death. Alternate translation: [he was taken by God to be with] or [God took his spirit to be with]

Make sure your translation of this phrase does not sound like these ancestors were still alive. They had already died before Abraham died. Alternate translation: [his relatives who had already died] or [his ancestors who had gone before him] or [his deceased relatives]

9.note: Alternate translation: [His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried his body]

See how you translated this phrase in Genesis 23:9, and see the note about that there. Also see how you translated similar phrases in Genesis 23:17, 19. Alternate translation: [in the cave of the Machpelah area]
Ephron no longer owned the field (See: verse 10).

For some languages it is clearer or more natural to put this phrase earlier in this verse. Also see how you translated **before Mamre** in Genesis 23:17, 19. Alternate translation: [near the city of Mamre]

10.note: The Hebrew text has two different ways to refer to the Hittites; compare the phrase here with verse 9 where a single Hebrew word is used to refer to this people group. See how you translated **the sons of Heth** in Genesis 23:20.

Abraham had already buried Sarah’s body in the cave (Genesis 23:19). Make sure your translation of this sentence does not sound like Sarah was buried there a second time. Alternate translation: [Abraham was buried in that cave, where his wife Sarah had also been buried] or [That is where Sarah had been buried, and they buried Abraham next to her]

11.note: Use the phrase order in your language that is most natural in this context.
Alternate translation: [who settled near] or [Isaac lived in the region near]
Be consistent here with how you spelled **Beer Lahai Roi** in Genesis 24:62. Alternate translation: [the well called Beer Lahai Roi]

12.note: Consider what is the best way in your language to introduce the new topic that begins here. See how you translated this clause in Genesis 11:10. Alternate translation: [Here is the genealogy of] or [Here is the list of the descendants of] or [What follows is the record of the descendants of]

13.note: Alternate translation: [listed in the order that they were born:]
Alternate translation: [His oldest child was Nebaioth]
Alternate translation: [After him came Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam]

15.note: See how you translated a similar list of names in verses 2–4.

16.q: וְ⁠אֵ֣לֶּה שְׁמֹתָ֔⁠ם בְּ⁠חַצְרֵי⁠הֶ֖ם וּ⁠בְ⁠טִֽירֹתָ֑⁠ם שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֥ר נְשִׂיאִ֖ם לְ⁠אֻמֹּתָֽ⁠ם
16.note: The Hebrew words for **settlements** and **camps** overlap in meaning. Both refer to temporary or permanent places where people settled, surrounded by some sort of wall or fence. Also, many translations have “princes” here instead of “rulers,” but these Ishmaelite rulers were not actually sons of a king. See how you translated **rulers** in Genesis 17:20. Alternate translation: [who became the rulers of twelve tribes that were named after them, and each tribe lived in its own settlements and camps] or [Each of them became the ruler of a tribe that was named after him, and each tribe had its own villages and tent settlements]

17.q: וְ⁠אֵ֗לֶּה שְׁנֵי֙ חַיֵּ֣י יִשְׁמָעֵ֔אל מְאַ֥ת שָׁנָ֛ה וּ⁠שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וְ⁠שֶׁ֣בַע שָׁנִ֑ים
17.note: See how you translated a similar sentence in verse 7.
See how you translated **exhaled** in verse 8. Alternate translation: [Then Ishmael breathed out for the last time and died] or [Then Ishmael took his final breath and died]
See how you translated this phrase in verse 8. Alternate translation: [and he was taken by God to be with] or [and God took his spirit to be with the spirits of]
Alternate translation: [his relatives who had already died] or [his relatives who had gone before him] or [his deceased relatives]

18.note: Be consistent here with how you spelled **Havilah** in Genesis 2:11; 10:7, 29 and **Shur** in Genesis 16:7; [20:1](ta:20). The name **Shur** means “wall.” The Wilderness of Shur may have been named after a city or fortification named Shur that was located near the eastern border of Egypt (Genesis 16:7). Alternate translation: [throughout the area that extended from the region of Havilah to the desert of Shur]
Alternate translation: [that is east of the land of Egypt]
Alternate translation: [as you go from there] or [as one goes]

Assyria and its capital city Asshur were far east of Shur. Consider again how you spelled **Asshur** in Genesis 2:14; 10:11, 22, and 25:3, 18. Alternate translation: [to the city of Asshur in Assyria] or [in the direction of the land of Assyria]

The meaning of this idiom is uncertain. It could mean: (1) “He lived in hostility toward all his brothers.” Alternate translation: [They lived as enemies against all their relatives] See how you translated a different idiom in 16:12 that probably has this meaning. Or it could mean: (2) “They settled in the presence of all their relatives.” Alternate translation: [They settled/lived among all their relatives]; (3) “He died in the presence of all his brothers.” Alternate translation: [Ishmael died in the presence of his brothers] or [Ishmael died while all his brothers were still alive]

19.note: We have already heard about much of Isaac’s history in previous chapters; now we are told even more. See how you translated **these are the generations of** in verse 12 and Genesis 6:9.
See how you translated **fathered** in verse 3. Alternate translation: [After Abraham had his son Isaac]

20.q: וַ⁠יְהִ֤י יִצְחָק֙ בֶּן־אַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה בְּ⁠קַחְתּ֣⁠וֹ אֶת־רִבְקָ֗ה & ל֥⁠וֹ לְ⁠אִשָּֽׁה
20.note: See how you translated “was a son of … years” in Genesis 21:5. Alternate translation: [Isaac grew up and married Rebekah when he was 40 years old]
Alternate translation: [She was a daughter of Bethuel, who was an Aramean from the land of Paddan Aram]
Alternate translation: [and she was a sister of Laban]

21.q: וַ⁠יֶּעְתַּ֨ר יִצְחָ֤ק לַֽ⁠יהוָה֙ לְ⁠נֹ֣כַח אִשְׁתּ֔⁠וֹ כִּ֥י עֲקָרָ֖ה הִ֑וא
21.note: Isaac and Rebekah had been married for almost 20 years and they still had no children. See how you translated **barren** in Genesis 11:30. Also, it may be clearer to change the order of the clauses in this sentence to put them in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [Isaac prayed earnestly to Yahweh for his wife to have children because she was barren] or [But for many years Rebekah was not able to get pregnant, so Isaac prayed that Yahweh would give her children]
Alternate translation: [Yahweh did what he prayed for]

For some languages it is clearer to include here the fact that Rebekah was pregnant with two babies, rather than wait until verse 22. Alternate translation: [so that Rebekah became pregnant with twins]

22.note: Alternate translation: [And the two babies inside her kept pushing against each other] or [After a while the twins wrestled with each other inside her]
Alternate translation: [What is happening inside me?]
Alternate translation: [Then she went to Yahweh to ask him what was happening] or [Then she prayed to Yahweh about it]

23.note: Many translations put Yahweh’s words in poetry format in this verse. If your translation team decides to do this, look at a Bible version that does this to know where to divide the clauses. Alternate translation: [Inside you are the ancestors of two people groups] or [The two babies inside your womb will become the fathers of two nations]
Alternate translation: [Those two people groups] or [Those two ancestors]
Alternate translation: [will be hostile against each other] or [will be rivals]
Alternate translation: [starting now even while they are still inside you]

24.note: Alternate translation: [Later when it was time for her to give birth]
Alternate translation: [sure enough, there were twin sons inside her!]

25.q: וַ⁠יֵּצֵ֤א הָ⁠רִאשׁוֹן֙ אַדְמוֹנִ֔י כֻּלּ֖⁠וֹ כְּ⁠אַדֶּ֣רֶת שֵׂעָ֑ר
25.note: Alternate translation: [When the first baby came out, he was covered with thick red hair so that he was as hairy as a fur robe] or [The first baby who was born was completely covered with thick red hair]
The Hebrew text has **they** here, which probably refers to Esau’s parents and may include people in general after his parents named him. Alternate translation: [So he was named]
Consider whether or not to include the meaning of Esau’s name in the text or in a footnote.

26.note: Some languages have a specific term for a younger brother that fits here. See what you did in Genesis 4:2.
See how you translated a similar clause in verse 25 that probably has the same meaning. Alternate translation: [So they called him] or [So he was named]
If you decide to include the meaning of Jacob’s name in the text or in a footnote, make sure it matches the way you translate **grabbing** earlier in this sentence.
See how you translated the idiom “was a son of … years” in verse 20.
Alternate translation: [when Rebekah gave birth to them]

27.note: Alternate translation: [As the boys grew up]
See how you translated a similar phrase **mighty hunter** in Genesis 10:9. Alternate translation: [Esau became a expert hunter] or [Esau became good at hunting animals for food]
Alternate translation: [and he preferred being in the open country] or [and he was an outdoorsman]

Make sure that it is clear in your translation that Esau and Jacob are being contrasted. Alternate translation: [but Jacob was a quiet man] or [Jacob, on the other hand, had a mild-mannered personality]
Alternate translation: [and worked close to home] or [and liked to be at home]

28.note: The author assumes that readers will know that both parents loved both sons. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. The translation should not sound as though Isaac and Rebekah did not love both of their sons. Rather, they each had their favorite son. Alternate translation: [Isaac loved Esau most]

Make sure your translation of **he liked** refers here to Isaac, not Esau. For some languages it is clearer or more natural to put this clause first in this sentence. Alternate translation: [Isaac liked to eat the meat of wild animals, so he favored Esau]
See how you translated a similar clause earlier in this verse. Alternate translation: [but Rebekah loved Jacob most]

29.note: According to verse 34, this stew (or thick soup) was made out of lentils, which are a type of bean; it may also have had pieces of meat in it. Consider what is the best way in your language to introduce the first event in this episode (following the background information in verses 27–28). Alternate translation: [Once Jacob was making some stew] or [One day when Jacob was making some stew]
See how you translated **field** in verse 27. Alternate translation: [Esau came home from working out in the fields]

The Hebrew word for **exhausted** means Esau was very tired (perhaps even feeling faint) from his hunting or work, as well as hungry and thirsty from lack of food. Some languages have an idiom for this that fits well here. Alternate translation: [and he felt weak from hunger] or [and he was weak and hungry] or [very tired and hungry]

30.note: Consider what is the best way in your language to translate this quote margin. Alternate translation: [So Esau asked Jacob]
Alternate translation: [some of that dark red stew you are making]
See how you translated **exhausted** in verse 29. Alternate translation: [because I am weak from hunger!] or [because I am hungry and weak!]
Frequently in the Hebrew text, this phrase has a general meaning and does not refer to someone specific. Alternate translation: [he is also called] or [they called him]
You could include the meaning of **Edom** in your translation or in a footnote so that it is clear why Esau was given that name.

31.note: Alternate translation: [But Jacob said to him]
Alternate translation: [Today right now] or [Right now]

32.note: Esau is using exaggeration here to emphasize how hungry he is. Consider what is the best way to communicate that in your language. Alternate translation: [Listen, I am so hungry that I feel like I am going to die!]

Esau uses a rhetorical question to emphasize his point about how hungry he is. Consider whether or not a rhetorical question works well here in your language. Alternate translation: [So how will my birthright benefit me if I die?] or [So my birthright is of no benefit to me right now!]

33.note: See how you translated “swear to me by God” in Genesis 21:23. Alternate translation: [First make an oath to me today before God that your rights are now mine!] or [You must first promise to me right now that you give your rights to me]
Make sure the way you translate this clause fits well with what Jacob just said. Alternate translation: [So he vowed to him] or [So Esau made an unbreakable vow to him]

See how you translated “sell your birthright” in verse 31. Also see how Hebrews 12:16 is translated, which refers to the same event. Alternate translation: [that he had sold his rights as the firstborn son to Jacob for the stew] or [that he was selling his firstborn-son-rights to him in exchange for the stew]

34.q: וְ⁠יַעֲקֹ֞ב נָתַ֣ן לְ⁠עֵשָׂ֗ו לֶ֚חֶם וּ⁠נְזִ֣יד עֲדָשִׁ֔ים
34.note: Consider again how you translated **stew** in verses 29 and 34. Lentils are small, round, flat, reddish-brown legume seeds that grow inside a pod (similar to peas or beans). If lentils are not known in your area, you could describe them as “a type of legume called lentils.” Alternate translation: [Then Jacob gave Esau some bread and some of the lentil stew] or [Then Jacob gave Esau some of the lentil stew with some bread]

Consider what is the most natural way to translate this series of actions that happened quickly one after the other and shows how carelessly Esau treated his birthright. Alternate translation: [and Esau ate, drank, stood up, and left] or [and Esau hurriedly ate the meal and left]

See how you translated **birthright** in verses 31–33. Alternate translation: [So Esau showed that he did not value his rights as the firstborn son] or [In that way, Esau treated his birthright flippantly, as if it had little value]
